title: The window is gone by the time you ask
spec: M28 · per-layer logging, replay debugging, alarms
intro: Accuracy slid seven points and the bill rose. With only answers logged, the best anyone can offer is "try a bigger model". With per-layer accounting, the same investigation takes one query and names the commit.

provenance.source: a narrated regression in a UCC risk pipeline; token counts, cache-hit rates, costs, and accuracy figures are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: This is M28's black box: log the shape of every context — per-layer tokens, cache-hit, cost, latency, version, guardrail flags — so a wrong answer becomes a replayable window instead of an anecdote.

steps.title: "The model must have changed"
narrative: Nightly eval accuracy on the UCC risk pipeline was 94% for two months. Last Tuesday it started coming back at 87%, and the invoice for the same request volume went up. Support has three complaints about liens the system missed.

You open the logs. There is one row per request: the request id, the question, the answer, and whether a human later marked it wrong. Nothing about what the model was shown. Every question worth asking — was the filing retrieved? where did it sit? did the cache hold? — is unanswerable from what was stored.

So the meeting produces the only hypothesis the data supports, which is not a hypothesis at all: the model must have changed, let's try a bigger one. That costs more and, if the cause is in your assembler, changes nothing.
steps.youDo: Open your own request log and try to answer one question: for a specific bad answer, how many tokens were in the retrieval layer? If you cannot, you have an accidental black box.

steps.title: Log the shape, not just the answer
narrative: The fix is one wrapper and it is boring on purpose. Around every model call, record the shape of the context: tokens per layer, the cache-read count the API already returns, cost, latency, model and prompt version, guardrail flags, tenant, request id — and a SHA-256 of the assembled context rather than the context itself, so you can prove two calls saw the same thing without storing a debtor's address in your log store.
None of this is inference. Every field is a number the assembler or the API response already has; you are simply refusing to throw it away.

The layer split is the load-bearing part. "11,900 input tokens" tells you nothing. system 5,200 · tools 1,900 · retrieval 3,100 · conversation 1,640 · question 60 tells you where the next regression will come from.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing about my call changed. The wrapper reads usage off the same response you were already discarding.
steps.youDo: Add @observe to your call site and log the per-layer dict your assembler already built. If your assembler concatenates strings and cannot name its layers, that is the first bug.

terminal.text: context_sha256 recorded · 5 layers accounted · cache stats captured · version stamped

steps.title: One query separates the two weeks
narrative: Now aggregate by layer across the good week and the bad one. Four of the five layers are flat to the token. The retrieval layer went from 3,100 to 9,400 — a retrieval top_k bumped from 5 to 12 in a config change on the Monday, which nobody connected to a Tuesday accuracy report.

Both symptoms fall out of that one number. Cost per request goes from $0.0204 to $0.0393 because 6,300 more uncached tokens are billed at full input price on every call — at 12,000 requests a week, $245 becomes $472.

And read the cache-hit line carefully, because it is the trap in this dataset. It fell from 60% to 39% and the cache never broke: the cached prefix is still exactly 7,100 tokens on every call. The rate dropped because the denominator grew. A metric moving is not yet a cause — which is precisely why you log the layers underneath it.
steps.youDo: Group your own logs by prompt version and diff the per-layer medians. A regression that is invisible in the total is usually obvious in one layer.

steps.title: Replay the window, then set the alarm
narrative: Cost is explained; accuracy is not. Seven more filings should help recall, not hurt it. So replay the exact window from req_8f21c4 — the log has the layer sizes, the retrieved filing ids, and their order.

There it is. The assembler sorts the retrieval block chronologically for readability. With five filings the disqualifying one, 2024-FL-0019988, sat at position 2. With twelve it sits at position 9 of 12 — the middle, the worst real estate in the window. It was retrieved every single time and read none of them. That is a positioning bug wearing a retrieval bug's clothes, and no amount of model-swapping would have touched it.

The fix is a rerank back to five, and the ordering rule moved from chronological to critical-facts-at-the-edges. But the durable output of this investigation is not the fix — it is the three alarms, because a metric you log and never watch is a metric you will read about on an invoice.
steps.claudeSays: The filing was in the window in both runs. In the second it was surrounded by eleven others in the position I attend to least.
steps.youDo: Take one wrong answer from last month, reconstruct its window from your logs, and find the ranked position of the fact it should have used. Do this before you change a single prompt.

3 alarms armed · the same regression now pages in under an hour, not in nine days

views.text: "The model is wrong" is not a bug report. "The retrieval layer tripled on Tuesday, the disqualifying filing moved from position 2 to position 9, and cost per request rose 93%" is one — and every clause of it came from fields the API had already handed you.
